explain: The first words of a two-line poem by Catullus about being torn about someone he loves. _ōdī_ looks like a past form, but means “I hate”: it is a verb that only has perfect forms.
distractors: _ōdit_ and _amat_ are “he hates and loves”. Catullus says “I”: _ōdī et amō_.

en: I do not love you, Sabidius.
explain: The first words of a famous epigram by Martial. _tē_ is the object (accusative) and _Sabidī_ is the person addressed, in the vocative.
distractors: _tū_ is nominative (“you” as the one acting). The one loved is accusative: _tē_.
_tibi_ is dative (“to you”). _amō_ takes the accusative: _tē_.
_amās_ is “you love”. Martial says “I do not love”: _nōn amō_.

explain: The next words in Martial's epigram. _quārē_ (why) is the word for the reason; _nec_ is “and not”; _possum dīcere_ is “I can say”.
distractors: After _possum_ the verb is an infinitive: _dīcere_, not _dīcō_.
_et_ is “and”: it would say “and I can say why”. Martial says “and not”: _nec_.

en: Oh, the times! Oh, the customs!
explain: Cicero's cry of dismay at the state of Rome, in his speech against Catiline. It is plural and in the nominative or accusative: _tempora_ (times), _mōrēs_ (customs, ways).
distractors: _tempus_ and _mōs_ are singular (“time” and “custom”). Cicero uses the plural.
_mōrum_ is genitive plural. Cicero's exclamation uses _mōrēs_.
_temporibus_ and _mōribus_ are dative or ablative. The exclamation uses the nominative: _tempora, mōrēs_.

explain: Literally “to whom (is it) for a good?”. A famous lawyer's question: look for the person who gains. Cicero quoted it from the judge Cassius. _cui_ is “to whom” and _bonō_ is dative.
distractors: _bonum_ is nominative or accusative. The saying has the dative: _bonō_.
_bonī_ is genitive or plural. The saying has the dative singular: _bonō_.

explain: Vergil's words in a pastoral poem. _omnia_ (everything) is the object, _amor_ is the subject (love), and the verb comes between them.
distractors: _amōrem_ is accusative. Love is the subject, nominative: _amor_.

en: It is sweet and honorable to die for one's country.
la: Dulce et decōrum est prō patriā morī.
explain: One of the most quoted lines of Horace. _prō_ (for) takes the ablative: _patriā_. _morī_ is “to die”. The adjectives _dulce_ and _decōrum_ are neuter: “(it is) a sweet and honorable (thing)”.
distractors: Dulce et decōrum est prō patriam morī.
Dulce et decōrum est prō patriae morī.
_patriae_ is genitive or dative. _prō_ takes the ablative: _patriā_.
Dulcis et decōrus est prō patriā morī.
_dulcis_ and _decōrus_ are masculine. Horace says “(it) is a sweet and honorable thing”, neuter: _dulce et decōrum_.

en: A man is a wolf to a man.
explain: A saying from a comedy of Plautus, meaning that people can be cruel to each other. _hominī_ is the dative: “to a man”.
distractors: _hominem_ is accusative. “To a man” is dative: _hominī_.
_hominis_ is genitive (“of a man”). “To a man” is dative: _hominī_.
_hominēs_ is plural (“men”). The saying has one man: _homō_.

explain: A proverb that goes back to Roman writers. _errāre_ is the infinitive (“to err”) and is the subject; _hūmānum_ is neuter, “(a) human (thing)”.
distractors: _errō_ is “I err”. The saying uses the infinitive: _errāre_.
_hūmānus_ is masculine. The saying calls it a “human thing”, neuter: _hūmānum_.
_hūmānō_ is dative or ablative. After _est_ the adjective is nominative: _hūmānum_.

explain: Catullus asks his Lesbia for “a thousand kisses”. _dā_ is the command “give”, _mihi_ is “to me”, and _bāsia_ is the plural of _bāsium_ (kiss).
distractors: _bāsium_ is singular (“a kiss”). A thousand kisses is plural: _bāsia_.
_dāte_ is a command to several people. Catullus speaks to one: _dā_.
